description: We are a passionate and collaborative team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We love technology, innovation, research, and solving real-world problems. Join us to share ideas, learn new skills, build something impactful, and enjoy the challenge together. We welcome members skilled in Development, AI/ML, UI/UX, Research, Data Analysis, Presentation, and Creative Thinking.
summary: ASTRAQUEST is a browser-based mission trainer game where kids command a Moon or Mars outpost and see how their choices play out over a simulated mission. It helps kids aged 7 to 12, with questions that adjust for older students, understand the real trade-offs of deep space survival, because astronauts must split limited resources and no choice is free. Players pick a mission length, a four-person crew out of 6 specialists, and a spacecraft. Divide resource units between power, life support, radiation shielding and food, and then handle each day's crises, where protecting one system leaves another to drain. Learners study each topic and pass a quiz before the mission, and the science is grounded in NASA data from ECLSS, NASA POWER, Curiosity RAD and NASA food-in-space research, which is credited inside the game.
details:
AstraQuest is an interactive, game-based web platform that teaches people about space exploration through real NASA science. Players take the role of a mission commander and choose a destination (the Moon or Mars). They buy rockets, crew and upgrades from a Space Store, then manage a spacecraft in real time as days pass on a mission clock.

Food, Radiation Shielding, Life Support and Power drain every simulated day. If a critical resource hits zero, the mission fails. Crisis alerts interrupt the mission on a schedule. In Space Food Rescue, players catch drifting food packets in a timed mini-game and then answer a five-question science quiz. In Oxygen Pipe Repair, they solve a repair challenge. Their combined score decides whether the crew recovers. Results feed a global leaderboard, and signed-in commanders have saved profiles, inventories and mission histories.

Alongside the game is a NASA Data hub with six topic areas: Rockets & Spacecraft, Space Food, Space Power & Energy, Space Basics, Astronaut Life, and Space Missions & Exploration. Each links to public NASA resources and is built from NASA data and the NASA API. A tutorial walks new players through how everything fits together. A machine learning layer adds data-driven insight to the experience.

Benefits and intended impact

Space science is often taught through dense text and passive lectures. AstraQuest turns it into decision-making. Players learn why astronauts need oxygen, food, shielding and power, and what happens when those systems fail, by dealing with the consequences themselves. Each crisis ends in a science check, so the learning is reinforced instead of left optional. We want to inspire curiosity in students and space enthusiasts, make NASA’s open data approachable for non-experts, and encourage more young people to see themselves in STEM and space careers. It runs in a browser, works for guests without an account, and is built to be accessible to a wide audience.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS and React.js, built and served with Vite
  • Backend: Django with the Django REST Framework, using token-based authentication (register, login, refresh)
  • Database: PostgreSQL for users, missions, results, store inventory and the leaderboard
  • Machine learning and data: Python with scikit-learn, NumPy and pandas
  • Data sources: the NASA API and a large collection of NASA datasets and public resources

What makes it creative

  • It combines a survival-style simulation with real NASA science. Mini-games and quizzes sit inside the story of a mission instead of being separate lessons.
  • Crises are scheduled once per mission and saved, so refreshing or resuming never rerolls the challenge.
  • The mission clock pauses when the tab is hidden, during alerts and during mini-games, so players never lose progress unfairly.
  • Mini-games support keyboard, touch and drag controls.
  • Guest play works locally, while signed-in players get persistent, cloud-saved progress.

Factors our team considered

  • Accuracy: educational content is grounded in real NASA data and resources.
  • Accessibility: it works on desktop and mobile, with multiple input methods and no account required to play.
  • Engagement vs. learning: the game loop has to be fun enough to keep players coming back while still teaching something.
  • Scalability and maintainability: a separate React frontend and Django API, tested without a database for fast checks, let the project grow with more missions, crises and datasets.
  • Fair, consistent gameplay: saved schedules, pausing logic and a leaderboard tied to real results keep play balanced.
